kurz: Why your own memory is the least reliable source when judging investment decisions, and which methods help more against this than good intentions.

bloecke.md:
“2008 was obviously foreseeable.” “It was clear that the recovery would come straight after the slump in March 2020.” Such sentences are easy to say and sound assured. Yet they are the main reason why investors often learn nothing from twenty years of stock market experience.

Baruch Fischhoff measured the effect in 1975. People who know the outcome of an event consider that outcome, in retrospect, to have been more likely than they had estimated beforehand. [[Hindsight bias]] works on three levels that reinforce one another. The memory of your own expectation shifts (“I had a feeling”), the event appears inevitable in retrospect (“it had to happen”), and this leads to the conclusion that it was predictable (“you could have seen it coming”). Nassim Taleb counts this after-the-fact illusion of explainability among the features of a black swan. Such an event lies outside expectations and has an extreme impact. Afterwards it looks like the logical consequence of warning signs that nobody added up in time.

bloecke.titel: MSCI World, annual returns 2012 to 2025 (gross, USD)
bloecke.unter: In retrospect the period looks like a decade of upward trend, but what investors lived through were three loss-making years and a gap of around 46 percentage points between the best and the worst year.

bloecke.md:
## Consequences of hindsight bias

The first consequence concerns position size. Investors who believe they spotted the last three turning points put more into the next bet. Hindsight bias, however, only increases confidence in your own forecasts; the ability to forecast stays unchanged. The larger stake therefore rests on confidence without the corresponding ability.

The second consequence is [[outcome bias]]. Here decisions are judged by their outcome instead of by the process. A soundly reasoned purchase that loses money counts as a mistake. A lucky hit that was not preceded by any thought counts as skill and is repeated. The result is a learning process that reliably reinforces the wrong habits.

The third consequence is a blockage of learning itself. Without a record, the memory of your own expectation is the least reliable source available. In a frequently cited survey of failed founders, a considerable proportion of those who had initially predicted success later no longer remembered this expectation. The DAX lost around 43.9% in 2002 and around 40.4% in 2008, and the MSCI World fell by around 57% between October 2007 and March 2009. Today each of these lows is described as an obvious buying opportunity, even though the news was at its bleakest on those days.

A decision is judged by what was known at the time it was made and how that knowledge was handled. The price three years later is no yardstick for this. This separation can only be maintained if what was known at the time was written down.

## Confirmation bias

In 1960 Peter Wason presented test subjects with the number sequence 2-4-6. They were to find the underlying rule by proposing sequences of their own for testing. Almost all of them guessed “plus two” and tested 8-10-12, 20-22-24 or 100-102-104, that is, exclusively sequences that could confirm their guess. The rule they were looking for was “ascending numbers”. By proposing 1-2-3, which fits the rule they were looking for but not “plus two”, the test subjects would have got further in a single move than with all their confirmations put together.

[[Confirmation bias]] works at three points. First it steers the search. People search for “XY share price target” and not for “XY share balance sheet risks”. Then it steers the interpretation. Good figures count as evidence, bad ones as an exceptional item, a one-off expense or a market overreaction. Finally it steers memory, and at this third point it has already become hindsight bias. The two biases therefore form a closed loop.

bloecke.unter: With each pass, conviction grows without any testable argument being added.

knoten.notiz: You read what agrees with you
Good figure = evidence, bad one = exception
The price says nothing about the thesis

bloecke.md:
## Recommendation systems and financial media

Today the bias arises without any effort of your own. Search and recommendation systems are designed to deliver more of what has already been clicked. Users who have twice watched a post about the imminent collapse of the financial system are shown the sequel the third time instead of a rebuttal. Financial media reinforce this, because exaggeration generates attention and attention is their business.

The law sets only a weak limit here. Under Article 20 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation (Regulation (EU) No 596/2014) in conjunction with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/958, persons who disseminate investment recommendations must present the information objectively and disclose their own interests and conflicts of interest. This also applies to posts on social networks, and BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) pursues violations. The disclosure, however, usually comes at the end and in the small print. Moreover, it changes nothing about which content reaches the user in the first place.

Disagreement is only useful in a particular form. It is not enough to read an opposing view. You have to be able to reproduce it in its strongest form before you evaluate it. Howard Marks's test question fits this. He asks whether a company is better than the price assumes, and not only whether it is good. An opinion that everyone shares is already reflected in the price and is therefore no reason to buy.

A critical article that you read in order to refute it strengthens your own thesis, because counter-evidence is scrutinised more harshly than supporting evidence. If what counts as a refutation is only decided afterwards, there is always a reason why a particular objection does not count. The criterion must therefore be fixed beforehand and exist in writing. Otherwise it can be shifted after the fact so that no objection applies any more.

## Forecasts without consequences

Year-end forecasts for stock indices are the most visible case. They are published in December, quoted in January and never checked afterwards. That keeps the forecasters in business. In addition, there is the listeners' hindsight bias, because in their memory the forecaster said roughly what then happened.

For the S&P 500, the track record of Wall Street strategists is documented. From 2018 to 2025 the consensus estimate was within plus/minus ten percentage points of the actual result in only a single year. In most of the past 16 years the return was underestimated. The largest single error went in the other direction. In 2022 the consensus expected plus 3.9%, the result was minus 19.4%, a deviation of 23.3 percentage points. Investors who tried to correct the errors mechanically would therefore be furthest off precisely in the years when it matters.

bloecke.unter: In the two documented years, the consensus was 23.3 percentage points too high in 2022 and around 21 percentage points too low in 2024 (figures as percentages).

bloecke.md:
## A written investment thesis as a precommitment

Against an error of memory, only an object outside memory helps. The investment thesis is a dated document drawn up before the purchase. It must contain three things: a claim about the future, a figure against which this claim can fail, and a date on which it is reviewed. If the criterion for refutation is missing, the document merely reflects a mood.

Warren Buffett keeps such records in public. In his shareholder letters he lists his own mistakes by name and amount. The purchase of the shoe manufacturer Dexter in 1993 ended in a total loss which, because it was paid for in Berkshire shares, grew to around $5.7 billion by 2014. Hesitating over the sale of the Tesco stake cost $444 million after tax. Such figures are only possible because the original reasoning exists in dated form and can no longer be smoothed over in retrospect.

bloecke.titel: Fields and wording of a written investment thesis
zeilen: What exactly is supposed to happen, and within what time
“Revenue growth of at least 8% p.a. until 2029, operating margin above 15%.”
“Net debt to EBITDA below 2.0 in every quarterly report.”
The event that refutes the thesis
“Falling revenue for two quarters in a row, or a margin below 12%.”
When the review takes place, in the calendar
“31 Mar 2027, date entered in the calendar”
Three sentences noted from the best opposing analysis, with source
“At most 3% of the portfolio, no further purchases without a new thesis.”

bloecke.md: On the review date, three questions are answered before the current price is looked at: whether what you claimed has happened, whether the refutation event has occurred, and whether you would open the position afresh today at this price. Only then is the price looked at. The order matters because a known price influences every answer to the first two questions.

Tax deadlines are the strictest form of precommitment, because nothing can be made up once they have passed. Under Section 20(6) EStG (Income Tax Act), losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from sales of shares, so they sit in a pot of their own. To offset such losses against gains at another bank, you need a loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung), which must be applied for by 15 December of the year in question (Section 43a(3) EStG). With the certificate, the loss carryforward at the issuing bank ends, and the offsetting takes place in the tax return via the capital income annex (Anlage KAP). Realising in January that you should have acted in December is hindsight in its purest form. Such deadlines should therefore be entered in the calendar.

When providing investment advice to retail clients, the institution must provide a suitability statement (Geeignetheitserklärung) on a durable medium before the transaction is concluded (Section 64(4) WpHG, Securities Trading Act). It gives written reasons why the recommendation matches the stated objectives, knowledge and circumstances. With the implementation of MiFID II in 2018, this document replaced the former advice record (Beratungsprotokoll).

In addition, there is the recording obligation under Section 83 WpHG. Telephone conversations and electronic communications relating to the receipt, transmission or execution of orders must be recorded, kept for at least five years and made available to the client on request.

Clients who received advice can therefore look up the reasoning given at the time and do not have to rely on their memory. With execution-only transactions through a direct bank or a neobroker, the normal case for an ETF savings plan, no such document is created. There, your own thesis exists only if you have written it down yourself.

## Bias blind spot

Behavioural research also describes the [[bias blind spot]]. Cognitive biases are reliably recognised in others and overlooked in yourself. Readers of this lesson will therefore spot hindsight and confirmation bias in every talk show, but still not in their own portfolio. So good intentions alone do not help. What works are objects and dates: a dated document, a review date entered in the calendar, a refutation noted in advance and a [[pre-mortem]] before every larger position. This takes around twenty minutes per decision and is the only approach that works regardless of how convinced you are at the moment.

mitnehmen: Hindsight bias changes the memory of your own earlier expectation and thereby removes the basis for any learning from experience.
Confirmation bias and hindsight bias form a cycle of steered search, steered interpretation and adjusted memory that can only be interrupted with aids outside your own memory.
An investment thesis without a refutation criterion and without a review date merely reflects a mood, even if there are figures next to it.

Forecasts have no consequences because nobody checks them afterwards, even though from 2018 to 2025 the consensus for the S&P 500 was within plus/minus ten percentage points in only one of eight years.
Decisions are measured by their process and outcomes by the account, because confusing the two rewards lucky hits and punishes good work.

begriffe.text: The retrospective overestimation of your own foresight. Anyone who knows the outcome remembers their own earlier expectation in a shifted form, considers the event inevitable and concludes from this that they have forecasting ability.

The tendency to seek out information preferentially, interpret it more favourably and remember it better if it fits your own thesis. Counter-evidence is scrutinised more harshly than supporting evidence.
Judging a decision by its outcome instead of by its process. In decisions under uncertainty it rewards lucky hits and punishes good reasoning.
The event, fixed in advance and in writing, whose occurrence refutes your own investment thesis. Without such a criterion, any thesis can be rescued after the fact.
Thought experiment before the decision. You assume that the position has turned into a disaster a few years from now and write down the reasons for it. This forces you to look for counter-evidence.
